conflicts.point: Whether upstream artificial intelligence developers possess the technical capacity to predict and constrain emergent safety failures prior to model deployment.

positions.stance: Upstream developers possess the ability to identify and mitigate systemic failure modes through rigorous pre-release auditing and alignment protocols.
Frontier model behaviors remain inherently unpredictable at the training stage due to emergent properties across countless downstream use cases.

conflicts.point: Whether output-based telemetry and runtime error monitoring provide sufficient operational visibility for insurers to price risk without inspecting model weights.

positions.stance: Surface telemetry fails to reveal systemic defects hidden within internal model weights, rendering external insurance pricing ineffective.
Execution-boundary monitoring of incident frequency and latency anomalies allows underwriters to price operational risk effectively under black-box constraints.

verdicts.conflict: Whether upstream artificial intelligence developers possess the technical capacity to predict and constrain emergent safety failures prior to model deployment.
verdicts.rationale: Both sides present coherent theoretical models of machine learning behavior but lack standardized, empirical metrics to prove whether frontier systems are fully controllable ex-ante. The debate currently relies on disputed projections rather than definitive audits from real-world deployments.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Longitudinal audit data from independent testing laboratories measuring pre-release predictability against actual post-deployment failure rates across multiple foundation models would settle this disagreement.

verdicts.conflict: Whether output-based telemetry and runtime error monitoring provide sufficient operational visibility for insurers to price risk without inspecting model weights.
verdicts.rationale: The skeptic position correctly identifies existing legal barriers, specifically commercial trade secrecy protections and non-disclosure agreements that legally block external actors from inspecting proprietary model weights. The opposing view asserts that surface telemetry works without explaining how underwriters can legally or technically bypass these trade secret protections.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Passing legislation that compels mandatory weight disclosure for commercial audits or the successful deployment of privacy-preserving cryptographic auditing tools that verify internal weights without exposing trade secrets would shift this balance.
